trig-unit-circle-angles-in-standard-posi.title: Angles in standard position
trig-unit-circle-angles-in-standard-posi.summary: Place directed angles and identify their terminal quadrants.

blocks.text: An angle in standard position has vertex at the origin and initial side on the positive x-axis. Counterclockwise rotation is positive; clockwise is negative. Terminal rays on coordinate axes are quadrantal, not inside any quadrant.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Angles in standard position. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: Always normalize when necessary and distinguish an axis from a quadrant.

blocks.title: Locate a directed angle
blocks.problem: Find the terminal quadrant of −135°.
blocks.strategy: Translate a clockwise rotation into a positive coterminal angle.
steps: 225° lies between 180° and 270°, so the terminal side is in Quadrant III.
blocks.check: 225° and −135° differ by 360°.

blocks.title: Quadrantal angle
blocks.problem: Where does the terminal ray of 630° lie?
steps: 270° points along the negative y-axis. It belongs to no open quadrant.

blocks.text: A 90° angle ends on the positive y-axis, not in Quadrant I or II.

blocks.prompt: What is the terminal quadrant of −30°?

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §1.1; Schaum’s Chs. 2, 6; Kelley Chs. 1, 4.

trig-unit-circle-quadrants-and-signs-of-.title: Quadrants and signs of functions
trig-unit-circle-quadrants-and-signs-of-.summary: Determine signs of all six functions in each quadrant.

blocks.text: On a radius-r circle, sinθ=y/r and cosθ=x/r. Tangent is y/x where x≠0; the reciprocal functions have the signs of their corresponding reciprocals. Coordinates on the axes require separate treatment.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Quadrants and signs of functions. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: Quadrant signs: QI (+,+,+); QII (+,−,−); QIII (−,−,+); QIV (−,+,−) for (sin,cos,tan).

blocks.title: Quadrant-II signs
blocks.problem: Determine the signs of sinθ, cosθ, and tanθ in quadrant II.
blocks.check: A quadrant-II point (−3,4) confirms the pattern.

blocks.title: Evaluate from a point
blocks.problem: The terminal side passes through (−5,−12). Find sinθ and tanθ.
blocks.strategy: Find r by the Pythagorean theorem.
blocks.check: Both coordinates are negative: sine negative, tangent positive.

blocks.text: Sine follows y; cosine follows x. Tangent is positive when x and y have the same sign.

blocks.prompt: Which trigonometric function is positive in Quadrant III: sine, cosine, or tangent?
blocks.explanation: In quadrant III both coordinates are negative, so y/x>0.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §§1.3–1.4, 2.2; Sullivan §2.3; Kelley Ch. 4.

trig-unit-circle-reference-angle-reducti.title: Reference-angle reductions
trig-unit-circle-reference-angle-reducti.summary: Reduce any-angle values using a reference angle and quadrant sign.

blocks.text: A reference angle α is the acute positive angle between the terminal ray and the x-axis. The magnitude of sinθ, cosθ or tanθ comes from α; its sign comes from the original quadrant. Reference-angle formulas must not erase the sign.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Reference-angle reductions. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: Shown for normalized 0°<θ<360° excluding quadrantal rays; for other angles first reduce modulo 360°.

blocks.title: Sine in QII
blocks.problem: Evaluate sin150° exactly.
steps: 150° is in Quadrant II, where sine is positive.

blocks.title: Cosine in QIII
blocks.problem: Evaluate cos225° exactly.
steps: Cosine is negative in quadrant III.
blocks.check: Point (−√2/2,−√2/2) lies in quadrant III.

blocks.text: Do not say sin(150°)=sin(30°) because the angles coincide; the equality follows reference angle and quadrant sign.

blocks.prompt: What is the reference angle for 315°?

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §2.2; Schaum’s Ch. 6; Kelley Ch. 4.

trig-unit-circle-exact-values-on-the-uni.title: Exact values on the unit circle
trig-unit-circle-exact-values-on-the-uni.summary: Recall standard-angle points and exact trig values throughout a revolution.

blocks.text: Unit-circle coordinates for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° follow special triangles. Reflect the first-quadrant magnitudes into other quadrants, using proper signs. At the axes some ratios are undefined.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Exact values on the unit circle. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: For exact values, preserve radicals rather than rounding decimal approximations.

blocks.title: Exact value in QIII
blocks.problem: Find sin240° exactly.
blocks.strategy: Reference angle 60°, sine negative in QIII.
blocks.check: The unit-circle y-coordinate is negative.

blocks.title: Find tangent on the circle
blocks.problem: Evaluate tan135° exactly.
blocks.check: Tangent is negative in QII.

blocks.text: Memorize first-quadrant coordinate patterns; derive the rest from symmetry and signs.

blocks.explanation: 300° is in QIV with reference angle 60°; cosine is positive.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §3.3; Young Chs. 2–3; Kelley Ch. 3.

trig-unit-circle-negative-and-coterminal.title: Negative and coterminal angles
trig-unit-circle-negative-and-coterminal.summary: Apply periodicity and parity to negative and multi-revolution angles.

blocks.text: The sine and cosine functions repeat every 2π radians; tangent repeats every π where defined. Cosine is even, sine and tangent are odd. These properties can reduce large or negative arguments to familiar values.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Negative and coterminal angles. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: Tangent periodicity applies only to arguments where tangent is defined.

blocks.title: Evenness of cosine
blocks.problem: Find cos(−60°).
blocks.check: The unit circle is symmetric about the x-axis.

blocks.title: Many rotations
blocks.problem: Find sin(−750°).
blocks.check: −750° and −30° are coterminal.

blocks.text: For negative angles, parity may be quicker than adding 360°.
Reference guide: Lial §§1.1, 2.2, 3.3; Kelley Ch. 4; Schaum’s Ch. 6.

trig-unit-circle-evaluating-functions-of.title: Evaluating functions of any angle
trig-unit-circle-evaluating-functions-of.summary: Evaluate all six trig functions at general angles using coordinates and identities.

blocks.text: For any terminal point (x,y)≠(0,0), define r=√(x²+y²)>0. Then sin=y/r, cos=x/r, tan=y/x; csc=r/y, sec=r/x, cot=x/y where denominators are nonzero. Always check undefined cases.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Evaluating functions of any angle. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: A terminal point may be anywhere except the origin. The coordinates need not lie on the unit circle.

blocks.title: All-angle ratios
blocks.problem: A ray passes through (−8,6). Find cosθ and cscθ.
blocks.strategy: Compute r, then use x/r and r/y.
blocks.check: Quadrant II: cosine negative, cosecant positive.

blocks.title: Undefined ratios
blocks.problem: Evaluate tan90° and sec90°.
blocks.strategy: At 90° the unit-circle x-coordinate is zero.
steps: tanθ=y/x and secθ=r/x both divide by zero.
Both are undefined, not infinite real numbers.
blocks.check: cos90°=0, so both quotient and reciprocal fail.

blocks.text: Compute r once; write all six ratios from x, y, and r.

blocks.prompt: If a terminal ray passes through (3,−4), find sinθ.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §1.4; Schaum’s Ch. 2; Kelley Chs. 3–4.

trig-graphs-domain-range-periodicity-and.title: Domain, range, periodicity, and symmetry
trig-graphs-domain-range-periodicity-and.summary: Identify domains, ranges, periods, parity, and key asymptotes.

blocks.text: Sine and cosine are defined on all real inputs, have range [−1,1], and period 2π. Tangent and secant are undefined where cosx=0. Cotangent and cosecant are undefined where sinx=0. A fundamental period is the smallest positive repeat interval.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Domain, range, periodicity, and symmetry. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: All statements use radian arguments; tangent equality applies where both sides are defined.

blocks.title: Domain of tangent
blocks.problem: Find the excluded x-values for tanx.
blocks.check: Vertical asymptotes occur at these excluded points.

blocks.title: Determine parity
blocks.problem: Classify y=sinx and y=cosx as even or odd.
blocks.check: Sine has origin symmetry; cosine has y-axis symmetry.

blocks.text: Periodicity does not make an undefined function value defined.

blocks.prompt: What is the range of cosx?
blocks.explanation: Unit-circle x-coordinates always lie between −1 and 1.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §4.1–4.4; Sullivan §§2.3–2.5; Young Ch. 4.

trig-graphs-sine-and-cosine-graphs.title: Sine and cosine graphs
trig-graphs-sine-and-cosine-graphs.summary: Sketch standard sine and cosine curves from their key points.

blocks.text: One period of y=sinx has values 0,1,0,−1,0 at x=0,π/2,π,3π/2,2π. Cosine begins at 1 and follows 1,0,−1,0,1. Plot anchors then connect smoothly; they have no sharp corners.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Sine and cosine graphs. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: Inputs on the horizontal axis are radians unless the graph states degrees.

blocks.title: Sine key points
blocks.problem: Give the five key coordinates of one standard sine period.
blocks.strategy: Divide the period into four equal parts.
blocks.check: The curve returns to y=0 after 2π.

blocks.title: Cosine key points
blocks.problem: Find cos(3π/2) and cos(2π).
blocks.strategy: Use horizontal coordinates on the unit circle.
blocks.check: These are the fourth and fifth standard cosine anchors.

blocks.text: Sine starts at the midline rising; cosine starts at its maximum.
Reference guide: Lial §4.1; Sullivan §2.4; Young Ch. 4; Kelley Ch. 5.

trig-graphs-tangent-and-cotangent-graphs.title: Tangent and cotangent graphs
trig-graphs-tangent-and-cotangent-graphs.summary: Sketch tangent and cotangent graphs with correct periods and asymptotes.

blocks.text: Tangent y=tanx has period π, zeros at x=kπ and vertical asymptotes at π/2+kπ. Cotangent y=cotx has period π, zeros at π/2+kπ and asymptotes at kπ. Within an interval between asymptotes tangent rises while cotangent falls.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Tangent and cotangent graphs. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.latex: \tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x},\quad\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x},\quad T=\pi
blocks.description: Exclude points with zero denominator; do not connect graph branches across asymptotes.

blocks.title: Tangent asymptotes
blocks.problem: Find tangent asymptotes on 0≤x≤2π.
steps: Therefore x=π/2 and 3π/2 are vertical asymptotes.
blocks.check: tan0=0 and tanπ=0 between branches.

blocks.title: Cotangent zeros
blocks.problem: Find all zeros of cotx in [0,2π].
blocks.check: At 0 and 2π cotx is undefined, not zero.

blocks.text: Mark asymptotes first, then zeros; tangent rises and cotangent falls.

blocks.prompt: What is the fundamental period of tanx?

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §4.3; Sullivan §2.5; Kelley Ch. 6; Schaum’s Ch. 7.

trig-graphs-secant-and-cosecant-graphs.title: Secant and cosecant graphs
trig-graphs-secant-and-cosecant-graphs.summary: Graph reciprocal trig functions using zeros of sine and cosine.

blocks.text: The secant curve consists of reciprocal cosine branches; cosecant consists of reciprocal sine branches. Both have ranges (−∞,−1]∪[1,∞). Secant is undefined when cosx=0; cosecant when sinx=0.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Secant and cosecant graphs. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: At graph points where the denominator is zero, draw asymptotes rather than values at ±∞.

blocks.title: Secant asymptotes
blocks.problem: Find the asymptotes of secx on [0,2π].
steps: secx has vertical asymptotes at those x-values.
blocks.check: sec0=1 and secπ=−1, so the branches reach ±1.

blocks.title: Cosecant extrema
blocks.problem: Evaluate csc(π/2) and csc(3π/2).
blocks.check: No cosecant value has magnitude less than 1.

blocks.text: Draw sine or cosine faintly first: reciprocal branches touch ±1 at peaks/troughs.

blocks.prompt: At what x in [0,2π] is cscx undefined?
blocks.explanation: Sine vanishes at integral multiples of π, so its reciprocal is undefined.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §4.4; Sullivan §2.5; Young Ch. 4; Kelley Ch. 6.

trig-graphs-amplitude-and-period.title: Amplitude and period
trig-graphs-amplitude-and-period.summary: Extract amplitude and period from a transformed sinusoid.

blocks.text: For y=A sin(Bx)+D or y=A cos(Bx)+D with nonzero A and B, amplitude is |A|, period is 2π/|B|, and vertical midline is y=D. A negative A reflects the curve rather than giving negative amplitude.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Amplitude and period. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: Amplitude and sinusoidal midline concepts apply to sine/cosine; do not assign tangent an amplitude.

blocks.title: Read a sinusoidal model
blocks.problem: For y=−3cos(2x)+1, find amplitude and period.
steps: Midline is y=1; reflection comes from A<0.
blocks.check: Maximum is 4 and minimum −2, centered on y=1.

blocks.title: Angular frequency
blocks.problem: For v(t)=5sin(100πt), find the frequency in hertz.
blocks.check: One cycle takes 20 ms.

blocks.text: Always use the absolute value of B in the period.

blocks.prompt: What is the period of y=sin(3x)?

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §4.1; Sullivan §§2.4,2.6; Young Ch. 4; Gibilisco Ch. 9.

trig-graphs-phase-shifts-and-vertical-tr.title: Phase shifts and vertical translations
trig-graphs-phase-shifts-and-vertical-tr.summary: Distinguish horizontal phase shifts from vertical translations.

blocks.text: For y=A sin(B(x−C))+D, the graph shifts horizontally by C and vertically by D, with period 2π/|B|. When written as A sin(Bx+φ)+D, the horizontal shift is −φ/B (assuming B≠0). Distinguish phase angle from time delay.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Phase shifts and vertical translations. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.latex: y=A\sin(Bx+\phi)+D\quad\Rightarrow\quad x_{\rm shift}=-\frac\phi B,\quad y_{\rm midline}=D
blocks.description: The shift −φ/B carries the units of x (radians for a graph versus seconds for time signals).

blocks.title: Identify a right shift
blocks.problem: Find the phase shift of y=2sin(x−π/3)+4.
steps: C=π/3, so shift right by π/3.
D=4, so midline moves up four units.
blocks.check: At x=π/3 the sine argument is zero.

blocks.title: Factor the inner coefficient
blocks.problem: Find the horizontal shift of y=sin(2x+π/2).
blocks.check: At x=−π/4 the sine argument is zero.

blocks.text: Factor the coefficient of x before reading the horizontal shift.

blocks.prompt: What is the horizontal shift of y=cos(3x−π)?

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §4.2; Sullivan §2.6; Young Ch. 4; Kelley Ch. 5.

trig-graphs-reflections-and-combined-tra.title: Reflections and combined transformations
trig-graphs-reflections-and-combined-tra.summary: Combine reflection, stretch, compression and translations in one graph.

blocks.text: In y=A f(B(x−C))+D, negative A reflects about the horizontal axis before vertical translation; negative B reverses the horizontal input. Sine and cosine combinations may admit equivalent phase-shift descriptions, so report the given chosen form clearly.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Reflections and combined transformations. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: The maxima/minima formula assumes sin/cos and A≠0. Horizontal reversal changes orientation but not the period.

blocks.title: Combined transformations
blocks.problem: Analyze y=−2sin(4(x−π/8))+3.
blocks.strategy: Read parameters directly from factored form.
steps: |A|=2; A<0 reflects the sine wave vertically.
C=π/8 is a right shift; D=3 gives midline y=3.
blocks.check: Midline 3 ± amplitude 2 gives 1 and 5.

blocks.title: Horizontal reversal
blocks.problem: Simplify y=cos(−2x) and find its period.
blocks.check: A cosine reflection across y-axis leaves the graph unchanged.

blocks.text: Track each transformation separately: A controls vertical scale/reflection, B period, C horizontal shift, D midline.

blocks.prompt: What is the range of y=−4cosx+2?

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §4.2; Young Ch. 4; Sullivan §2.6; Kelley Ch. 5.

trig-graphs-finding-an-equation-from-a-g.title: Finding an equation from a graph
trig-graphs-finding-an-equation-from-a-g.summary: Construct sine or cosine equations from graph features.

blocks.text: For sinusoidal data, estimate maximum M, minimum m, period T, and a convenient anchor. Then A=(M−m)/2, D=(M+m)/2, |B|=2π/T. Choose cosine at a maximum or sine at a midline crossing, accounting for phase.

blocks.caption: Illustrative diagram: Finding an equation from a graph. Use the specific problem data when solving.

blocks.description: Different sinusoidal equations may represent the same curve; check key points and the stated time/angle units.

blocks.title: Model from a maximum
blocks.problem: A curve has max 7, min 1, period π, and a maximum at x=0. Give a cosine equation.

blocks.title: Model a rising midline crossing
blocks.problem: A sinusoid crosses y=1 rising at x=0; amplitude 2, period 4π. Find a sine model.
blocks.check: At x=0, y=1 and derivative is positive.

blocks.text: Use a positive A when possible by choosing a convenient starting maximum or rising midline.

blocks.prompt: A sinusoid has max 9 and min 3. What is its amplitude?
blocks.explanation: Amplitude is half the vertical span: (9−3)/2=3.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial §§4.1–4.2; Sullivan §2.6; Young Ch. 4; Kelley Ch. 5.
